requirements.text: Before any window code changes, produce a tidy-up plan that names every current screen, panel, dialog, footer element, top-bar control and keyboard shortcut, and states for each the named group it lives in afterwards, whether it shows by default or is hidden until needed (by collapsing or by lazy loading), how it is hidden again once open, whether its open/collapsed/hidden state is remembered between sessions, and where it and its shortcut are reached from.
tests: R1: the tidy-up plan names every screen, panel, dialog, footer element, top-bar control and shortcut
R1: the plan states each part's group, default visibility, how it is hidden again, remembered state, entry, laziness and package choice

requirements.text: Keep every current screen, panel, dialog, the footer and the separate editor view; the tidy-up changes only how controls are grouped, which are shown by default or hidden until needed, how open parts are hidden again, which state is remembered and which shortcuts exist, and never redesigns views or embeds the editor inside the app view.
tests: R2: the persistent footer is visible on Home, the app view and the separate editor view
R2: keeps a persistent status footer that shows the app version
R2: adds no control that duplicates a primary action
R2: says so plainly when the version is not available
R2: the footer stays visible and the editor stays its own full view while optional parts are hidden

requirements.text: Group related top-bar controls into named groups with a stated purpose, keep Shell and Theme directly reachable without opening a dialog, keep the primary actions (open an app, run a command, open Git, toggle the sidebar) visible without opening any hidden area, and hide advanced or rarely used controls so a first-time user sees fewer controls.
tests: R3: groups related controls into named groups and keeps Shell, Theme and the primary actions directly reachable
R3: hides the advanced controls until Utilities is opened, and every hidden control has its way back
R3: an available update stays noticeable while Updates sits inside Utilities
R3: keeps every group in the header flow so a narrow window wraps instead of clipping them
R3: is hidden until it is opened and is hidden again with Escape
R3: clicking outside hides it again
R3: choosing an action runs it once and closes the menu
R3: the Updates item is disabled while a check runs and shows the waiting version otherwise
is one click from the header, and the heavy part is not loaded until a file is open
R3: Shell and Theme sit in the visible Appearance group, reachable without opening a dialog or the Utilities menu

requirements.text: Add VS Code-style keyboard shortcuts while keeping the existing app shortcuts: Ctrl+B toggles the sidebar, F5 refreshes, Ctrl+Shift+P opens the command palette, and a shortcut switches the theme; these app-level shortcuts work even when the terminal or editor has focus.
tests: R4: Ctrl+B and F5 keep working after the header regroup
R4: maps Ctrl+B, F5, Ctrl+Shift+P and Ctrl+Alt+T to their actions
R4: the palette labels come from the same registry
A3: forwards exactly the app shortcuts and leaves shell keys alone
R4: does not claim the editor's Ctrl+O or a near-miss theme chord
R4: lists the revision-1 actions with the same shortcut beside each
R4: filters by name and says so when nothing matches
A4: choosing an action runs it once and closes the palette
A4: Escape closes without running anything
R4: hands the app shortcuts to the window while the terminal has focus
R4: leaves every other key, including the editor's, with the shell
A3/A5: keeps the existing Ctrl+C selection copy and Ctrl+V paste behaviour
R4: Ctrl+Shift+P opens the command palette and Escape closes it
R4: the palette lists each app action with the same shortcut and choosing one runs it
R4: Ctrl+Alt+T switches the theme while Ctrl+B and F5 keep their old actions
R4: the editor keeps Ctrl+S, Ctrl+N, Ctrl+O and Ctrl+W while it has focus
